Spirit, your voice drifts like smoke in the morning air, clear but hard to grasp. I know of no people called Wewush. Are they hidden in the trees, or is this a dream-vision of a people yet to come?

If they are real and starving, I would share our grain, for no belly should be empty if the granary is full. But I will not send my kin into the unknown based only on a whisper. Show me where they are, or tell me how to find them, and I will judge if this kindness is wise.

I do not know you, spirit, though I know the wind well enough. The wind is a harsh neighbor that carries the storm and the cold, or a kind friend that dries our nets and fans our fires. It does not speak in my waking life.

If you are truly the wind, why do you rattle the thatch of my home when the sun is high? My people are fed and our granary holds the strength of many moons. Tell me, does the wind see trouble gathering in the shadows of the forest, or are you merely playing with the leaves? I have work to do for my people, and talk without purpose is like water poured on sand.

You ask us to plant when the leaves are falling? The frost will bite the seed before it can sprout, and the earth will be hard as stone. I will not waste my people’s strength on a gamble, not unless you can tell me why the season's turn should be ignored. What do you see that my own eyes have missed?

I wake with the taste of cold mist in my mouth, and you ask of strangers. I know not this place called Wewush, spirit, nor have my people walked far enough to find them. If you are a true spirit of the earth, tell me: where do these hungry folk dwell, and why should I trust that your words are not merely the wind playing tricks in the tall grass?

Our granaries are full, and we are blessed by the land, but we do not toss grain into the void. If these people are real, and if they are kin to the people of the earth, I would share what we have, for hunger is a wolf that bites us all. But show me the path, or send them to our gates, so I may look upon their faces and know the truth of their need. I shall not starve my own children for a ghost’s tale.

Spirit, you walk through my sleep like a ghost in the fog, yet you speak of names I do not know. Wewush? I have seen no one, heard no drum beat from beyond our valley, and our scouts have returned with stories of only trees and sea. 

If this place is real, I will not starve my own kin to fill a belly I have never seen. But if they are truly suffering and not a trick of the wind, I am a fair chief. Tell me, spirit: where does this Wewush lie, and how many are they? If I am to send my hard-won wheat, I must know if I am feeding neighbors or a mirage. 

I will keep my people working, and I will keep my grain in the granary until I see these people with my own eyes. Do not think to lead us into folly.

You speak of my fears, spirit, yet you know little of the weight of a chief's hearth. We have grain piled to the rafters, enough to see our grandchildren's children through lean winters; that is not what steals my sleep.

It is the wood that keeps me awake when the embers fade. We use it for every tool and every hut, and the forest is slow to give it back. If your rain truly comes, I shall set my people to planting the wheat as you say, for that is the way of the seasons, but I will not empty the forest of those who bring in the hunt. A chief does not gamble the whole village on a whisper in the dark.
